questions.stem: Which three phases comprise the Utterback-Abernathy model?
questions.explanation: The Utterback-Abernathy phases are fluid, transitional, and specific. Memorise this exact terminology.

questions.stem: In the fluid phase, the rate of product innovation is _____ and the rate of process innovation is _____.
questions.explanation: Fluid phase: high product innovation (many competing designs), low process innovation (no point in optimising a production line for a design that may not win).

questions.stem: A dominant design is best defined as:
choices: The most technologically advanced product in a market.
A single product architecture accepted by the market as the de facto standard.
The product with the largest market share.
The product with the lowest unit cost.
questions.explanation: Dominant design = de facto architectural standard. It need not be the best technology; it must bundle enough features at acceptable cost for the broad market.

questions.stem: Which is the textbook example of a dominant design in automobiles?
questions.explanation: The Model T established petrol-engine, four-wheel, front-engine, steering-wheel architecture as the dominant car design after 1908.

questions.stem: Which phase is characterised by industry shake-out and the crossover of product and process innovation curves?
questions.explanation: The transitional phase is where dominant design emerges, weak players exit, process innovation accelerates, and the two innovation-rate curves cross.

questions.stem: In the specific phase, competition is mainly based on:
questions.explanation: Once architecture is locked, firms compete on operational efficiency: cost, quality, and brand. Capital intensity rises and entry barriers harden.

questions.stem: VHS beat Betamax primarily because:
choices: JVC built a wide licensee coalition and locked in complementary assets (rental shops, content), creating stronger network effects.
VHS was patented and Betamax was not.
questions.explanation: Betamax arguably had better technical quality. VHS won on ecosystem: open licensing, longer recording time, and rental-shop standardisation produced decisive network effects.

questions.stem: Why is first-mover advantage typically WEAK in the fluid phase?
choices: First movers often pick the wrong architecture and lose to fast followers who learn from their mistakes.
Patents do not apply in the fluid phase.
Capital is scarce for first movers.
questions.explanation: In the fluid phase no one knows which design will win. Early commitments are bets, and many lose. Apple, Google, Facebook were all fast followers, not first movers.

questions.stem: Which industry is currently best classified as in the fluid phase?
questions.explanation: Humanoid robots show many competing architectures (Tesla Optimus, Figure, 1X), unclear customer use case, no dominant design — textbook fluid phase.

questions.stem: Smartphones today are best classified as:
questions.explanation: The dominant design (rectangular slab, capacitive touch, app store, two OSes) is locked. Innovation is incremental; competition is on cost, brand, and ecosystem. Specific phase.

questions.stem: Which is NOT a typical characteristic of the fluid phase?
choices: High capital intensity and large oligopolistic firms
questions.explanation: High capital intensity and oligopoly belong to the specific phase. Fluid-phase firms are small, organic, and capital-light.

questions.stem: The QWERTY keyboard is a frequently cited example of:
choices: A dominant design that locked in despite alternatives like Dvorak that are arguably superior
questions.explanation: QWERTY illustrates that dominant designs are about lock-in, not technical superiority. Switching costs and installed base keep it dominant.

questions.stem: Electric vehicles are best placed in which phase today?
choices: Transitional — a dominant design (skateboard battery, OTA updates, big touchscreen) is emerging but not locked
questions.explanation: EV designs are converging on skateboard battery + dual-motor + software-defined cabin, but several architectural choices (e.g. battery chemistry, charging standards) are still being settled.

questions.stem: At the point a dominant design emerges, you would expect:
choices: An increase in the number of competing firms.
An industry shake-out, with many fluid-phase players exiting or being acquired.
A drop in process innovation rate.
questions.explanation: Dominant design causes a shake-out: firms that bet on losing architectures exit, and surviving firms scale up production.

questions.stem: Which of the following is a key role of a dominant design?
choices: It crystallises user expectations and standardises component interfaces, enabling cumulative learning.
It eliminates the need for patents.
It guarantees the technologically best solution.
It marks the start of the fluid phase.
questions.explanation: Dominant designs lock interfaces, allowing suppliers, complementors, and customers to invest with confidence. This enables learning-curve effects.

questions.stem: A common LIMITATION of the Utterback-Abernathy model is that:
choices: It only applies to American firms.
It fits assembled physical products better than software-as-a-service or multi-sided platforms.
It is incompatible with Christensen's framework.
questions.explanation: The model was built from manufacturing data. SaaS and platforms have business-model dominant designs, not architectural ones, and the curves do not map cleanly.

questions.stem: A 'standards war' typically occurs in which phase?
choices: Fluid, where multiple competing architectures fight to become the dominant design
Specific, where firms compete on cost
After the specific phase, in industry decline
questions.explanation: Standards wars (VHS/Betamax, HD-DVD/Blu-ray, GSM/CDMA) define the late fluid / early transitional phase before a dominant design locks in.

questions.stem: Process innovation overtakes product innovation in importance in which phase?
questions.explanation: The crossover happens in the transitional phase, near the emergence of the dominant design. By the specific phase, process innovation dominates but both rates are declining.

questions.stem: A digital camera disrupting film photography is best described as:
choices: A specific-phase incumbent extending its lead.
A disruption that reset the film industry back to a fluid phase under a new technology.
Process innovation within the film industry.
questions.explanation: Specific-phase industries can be reset to fluid by a new technology stream. Digital photography reset the dominant design for image capture.

questions.stem: Which is the best diagnostic question to determine an industry's phase?
choices: Is there a dominant design? If yes, are firms competing on cost?
How many patents have been filed?
What is the average firm age?
questions.explanation: The dominant-design status plus the basis of competition (architecture vs cost) is the cleanest two-question diagnostic for fluid/transitional/specific.

questions.stem: Capital intensity is HIGHEST in which phase?
questions.explanation: Specific-phase firms invest heavily in dedicated production lines, automation, and tooling optimised for the dominant design. Fluid-phase firms keep capital low to preserve optionality.

questions.stem: Which of the following best supported VHS's win in the videotape standards war?
choices: Open licensing to multiple manufacturers, longer recording time, and rental-shop standardisation.
Lower retail price than Betamax at launch.
questions.explanation: Sponsor coalition + complementary assets + a feature that mattered to customers (recording length for a full movie/sports event). Network effects then locked it in.

questions.stem: Which statement about fluid-phase customer behaviour is correct?
choices: Customers know exactly what they want and demand low prices.
Customer needs are unclear; users do not yet know what they want or how to compare offerings.
Customers refuse to adopt until standards exist.
questions.explanation: Fluid-phase customers are exploratory. They are willing to try variants and learn alongside vendors. Brand and standards come later.

questions.stem: Which framework BEST complements Utterback-Abernathy for explaining how incumbents are displaced by new entrants?
questions.explanation: Utterback-Abernathy describes industry dynamics; Christensen explains why incumbents specifically fail. They are commonly paired in essay answers.

questions.stem: The IBM PC (1981) is cited as a dominant design because:
choices: It had the fastest CPU at launch.
It bundled Intel x86, MS-DOS, and open expansion slots — an architecture the market converged on.
It was vertically integrated end-to-end by IBM.
It outsold the Apple II in its first year.
questions.explanation: Open architecture + a coalition of complementors (clone makers, software developers) cemented the IBM PC as the dominant design and ironically eroded IBM's own position.
